Introducing AvRate - a new way to look at batters.

AvRate: Why the Greats Need Both - The oldest argument on the grass bank Every cricket ground has two kinds of fan. One quotes averages like scripture. The other wants to know how quickly the runs came, and whether anyone stayed awake for them. At The Grass Bank, those two fans have names.

IJ
Ivan Joseph The Grass Bank™ Opinion
November 18, 2026

The oldest argument on the grass bank

Every cricket ground has two kinds of fan. One quotes averages like scripture. The other wants to know how quickly the runs came, and whether anyone stayed awake for them.

At The Grass Bank, those two fans have names. Cranky swears by average: runs per dismissal, the purest measure of a batter's worth. Banky points out that a hundred off 400 balls and a hundred off 150 balls are not the same day's cricket.

They are both right. They are also both wrong. This piece is about why, and about the simple fix we call AvRate.

Average: necessary, not sufficient

Average tells you how many runs a batter scores before getting out. It rewards patience, technique and the stubborn refusal to leave. It is the backbone of Test cricket, and Cranky is right to love it.

But average is blind to time. A Test lasts five days, and a team needs twenty wickets to win. Runs that arrive too slowly can leave your bowlers with no time to finish the job. Two batters can both average 50, and one of them wins you Tests while the other saves them.

Saving Tests is honourable work. But if average were the whole story, we would rank a batter who blocks out a draw alongside one who sets up a declaration on day four. Nobody in the stands believes that, not even Cranky, at least not out loud.

Strike rate: thrilling, but fickle

Strike rate tells you how many runs a batter scores per 100 balls. It measures pressure: on the bowler, on the field, on the clock. It is why some batters empty the bars and others empty the stands. But strike rate by itself is blind to survival. A batter who smashes 30 off 20 balls and then holes out to long-on has a gorgeous strike rate and a team that is 60 for 4. In a Test, a quick 30 is a cameo. A quick 150 is a match-winner. Strike rate cannot tell them apart. If strike rate were the whole story, the greatest Test batter of all time would be whoever swings hardest at the first ball. Banky would be the first to tell you that is how you end up watching the second session from the dressing room. If we go to the basics of the game, between two players, if one can only defend a ball but the other can hit that same ball, the latter is the better bat IF he can also bat for a long time. Now if he bats for a long time, it naturally follows that he will also have a high average. So what should we do?

AvRate: add them up

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple:

{AvRate} = {Batting average} + {Strike rate}

That is it. No weights, no regression, no PhD. As Banky likes to say, even selectors can do it.

AvRate rewards the batter who stays in and keeps the scoreboard moving. A long stay at a crawl scores well on one half and poorly on the other. A dashing cameo does the reverse. Only the batters who do both, for a whole career, rise to the top.

Figures from The Grass Bank's Compare page.

Look at the middle of the table. Kallis, Dravid and Chanderpaul all average more than Richards, Sehwag and Gilchrist. On average alone, Cranky would rank them higher. Yet nobody watching those careers felt Chanderpaul tilted a Test the way Richards did. AvRate explains the gut feeling: Richards matched their staying power and scored at least 40% faster.

Now look at Lara and Tendulkar, the defining rivalry of their era. Their averages are almost identical, 52.89 and 53.79. AvRate breaks the tie in Lara's favour, by more than five points, because he scored his runs a little quicker. Argue with that in the comments, by all means. Cranky already has.

None of this makes Dravid or Kallis lesser cricketers. They were among the best ever at their job, which was often to make sure their team did not lose. AvRate simply asks a different question: who did the most to help their team win?

So who are the best ever by this metric?

Here's a look at the top 20 of all time. To remove those who had short careers and excelled in one but not in the other, I have used 3000+ runs in 50+ innings with an average of 45+. Based on this we get the following list of players:

Sir Don is on top, which shouldn't really surprise anybody because an average on 99.94 gives him a boost that nobody else can even aspire to match even though on strike rate alone 8 of the top 20 are ahead of him. However it is Harry Brook at no 2 that should make people take notice. His career so far has been nothing short of remarkable and by this metric he is the second greatest ever. His career is far from over so we can make a definitive judgement only after he retires but by golly, he is up there.

Sehwag is at #3 all time, ahead of India's favorite son Sachin. This will be a great debate in coffee shops around the world but to have an average that is not very far from Sachin's and a strike rate that is about 28 points higher makes him stand well ahead of Sachin. He played over 100 tests too so to have maintained this over such a long period is nothing short of outstanding.

We have Gilly rubbing shoulders with Richards and Lara and that might be a position well earned! We also see Kevin Pietersen in this list and deservedly so even ahead of Joe Root. Both greats of the game but this could be another one for the coffee shop.

Sachin is sandwiched between Graeme Smith and Gary Sobers, Williamson is ahead of AB and Clarke ahead of Greg Chappell. The traditionalists like Cranky will probably shake their heads but Banky might look at this and say cool!

It is also quite revealing that in this top 20 list there are seven Australians. They also have the best winning record in international cricket and that cannot be merely a coincidence.

England's top five:

Three modern day greats and two old timers make up this elite list. Brook is far ahead of everyone else at the moment, KP and Root are neck and neck and Root might be able to get into second spot before he hangs up his boots. Hobbs and Hammond were not particularly fast scorers but make up with very impressive averages. Also they are all above 100 points in total which is a number worth keeping in mind as we look at other countries.

India's top seven:

There is one surprise but it shouldn't be because he was exceptionally gifted - Mohammad Azharuddin slots in at 3 just below Sachin and ahead of Kohli by a whisker! Sunny rounds out the top 5 because he is the only one in this group with a sub 50 SR. The admirable Dravid and that wristy magician Laxman miss out but they are just below with Laxman at 6 ahead of Dravid because of his higher strike rate which more than compensates for his lower average. It is pertinent to point out that the top 4 all have SR's well in excess of 50 while the other 3 are below, which also puts them below the 100 point mark. Great players, all of them but this does provide a different way to look at them and of course Sehwag stands out as the absolute outlier!

New Zealand's top five err top two:

The kiwis have only two based on the filters we have chosen but I don't think anybody will dispute these names, both of whom are legitimately their greatest players. Not much of a debate here but I can see folks nodding their heads silently.

Pakistan's top five:

No surprises really and similar to NZ, there is unlikely to be a debate about them. Miandad fans might think he should be higher and that argument would be a good one to have.


South Africa's top five:

In this case we are going to relax the minimum innings (no minimum) and minimum runs (1000+) criteria given their exclusion from the world stage for about two decades. Graeme Pollock stands tall here, Smith may be a bit of a surprise but his numbers are exceptional with the highest SR among all of them and so fully deserves his position. AB is a surprise at 3 given the expectation that with his ability he would have a very high SR but in tests he didn't bat as explosively as he could so we can only assume that he chose to rein himself in

Sri Lanka's top 3:

Like NZ, SL only has 3 players who meet the standards that the filters have imposed. The only surprise is that Aravinda De Silva does not feature in this list. There is no doubting the fact that he was one of the greats but his average of 43 puts him below the cut line so he sadly misses out.

West Indies top 10:

There were some glaring omissions in West Indies top 5 (the 3W's) so I expanded the list to the top 10 and we can see why they were not in the top 5. For Walcott and Weekes, the SR data is not available. The highest average among all these greats in fact belongs to Everton Weekes (see the other story "Meeting Everton Weekes" ) so it would be doing a disservice if I excluded them.

There should be no debate about the top 2 though - Viv and Lara belong right at the top. The fierce debate that I can see raging is - which one of them is greater. Numbers don't lie but the evidence of your eyes is often a higher truth. (Also see GOAT vs GILT, for more on this)

What do you think? The comments page is open.

Does it survive the statisticians?

At this point a statistician usually clears their throat. "You can't just add two different numbers together." It's a fair objection, so let's take it seriously.

Same currency. Both numbers are measured in runs. Average is runs per dismissal; strike rate is runs per 100 balls. Adding them is less like adding apples and oranges, and more like adding two kinds of apple.

Similar scales. For established Test batters, averages mostly sit between about 35 and 60, and strike rates between about 40 and 85. Because the two ranges are similar, neither number drowns out the other. If strike rate ran into the thousands, addition would be silly. It doesn't, so it isn't.

A clear trade-off. Under AvRate, one extra run of average is worth exactly one extra point of strike rate. You may prefer a different exchange rate, but this one is transparent, easy to check, and treats both skills as equally important. When there is no strong reason to favour one over the other, equal weighting is the honest default.

More is always better. Raise either number and AvRate goes up. It never punishes a batter for being better at something.

Why not multiply? Multiplying average by strike rate is another option, and it has its fans. But multiplication amplifies extremes: a very high number on one side can carry a weak number on the other. Addition is more forgiving of small errors and harder to game.

AvRate is not a law of nature. It is an index, a simple and honest summary of two things that matter. Like any index, it is only as good as the questions you ask of it, which brings us to the fine print.

The fine print

Every good formula comes with a warning label. Here is ours.

The Afridi problem. Shahid Afridi averaged 36.51 in Tests at a strike rate of 86.97. That gives him an AvRate of 123.48, ahead of Viv Richards. Boom Boom would enjoy that. Viv would not. A thrilling cameo player can rack up AvRate on strike rate alone, so AvRate needs a qualifying bar: we suggest at least 3,000 Test runs and an average of 40 or more. Below that, you are measuring fireworks, not a career.

The Bradman problem. Balls faced were not recorded for every innings in the early decades of Test cricket, so strike rates for older players are estimates or simply unknown. The Don's AvRate is a matter of educated guesswork. By most accounts he scored quickly, so it would be enormous, but we can't print a number we can't stand behind.

The era problem. Test scoring has sped up over time. A strike rate of 60 meant more in the 1980s than it does in the age of Bazball. AvRate is fairest when it compares batters from the same era, or when each number is measured against its era's norm.

The last word

Average tells you whether a batter will stay. Strike rate tells you whether the stay will matter. The true greats did both, for years, against the best bowlers of their time. That is what separates a Richards or a Lara from the merely very good, and AvRate is our simple way of saying so.

Banky, naturally, gets the last word: "Add them up. Even selectors can do it."

Cranky, naturally, gets the last grumble: "Fine. But I'm still right.
